David Hume. He lived from 1711 to 1776 and was a Scottish Enlightenment philosopher whose radical empiricism and skeptical questioning of causation, morality, and religion profoundly shaped modern philosophy. Applying empirical reasoning to domains where rationalism had previously dominated, Hume demonstrated that fundamental beliefs about cause-and-effect, the self, and divine necessity cannot be rationally justified by experience alone, forcing later thinkers to reckon with the limits of human knowledge.

Hume's central argument about causation was revolutionary. We never observe causation itself, he argued. We only observe the constant conjunction of events—A is always followed by B. Our belief in causal necessity is not a rational conclusion from experience but a habit of mind. He applied this skeptical method to the self as well, arguing that introspection reveals not a unified self but a bundle of perceptions in constant flux. Personal identity is not a metaphysical fact but a pragmatic fiction created by memory and resemblance.

On morality, Hume argued that reason alone cannot motivate action. Morality must be grounded in sentiment—in sympathy, benevolence, and fellow-feeling—not in rational principle. This was a radical departure from rationalist ethics. His Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, published after his death, presented sophisticated critiques of the design argument for God's existence. These dialogues showed that belief in divine providence cannot be rationally justified from observation of nature's disorder and suffering.

Hume formulated what became known as Hume's fork, a distinction between relations of ideas and matters of fact. Relations of ideas include mathematical and logical truths, knowable a priori without needing to check the world. Matters of fact are empirical claims, knowable only through experience. This fork became foundational to modern epistemology and philosophy of science. Immanuel Kant famously said that Hume interrupted his dogmatic slumber and inspired Kant's critical philosophy, though Kant tried to rescue metaphysics from Humean skepticism. Hume was a naturalist who applied empirical observation and psychological reasoning to explain how the human mind works, essentially founding modern psychology and cognitive science.
